lead: The me I picture and the me others see may not be the same picture.
when: When team members' assessments of each other differ widely, "I thought you knew" keeps coming up, or you want useful feedback or to explain what you need to work well together.
body:
You think you're an active participant in meetings, but your coworkers feel you often cut them off. You think people know you're not good at speaking on the spot, but you've never actually told them. Some gaps in communication come from the two sides having different information, not just from someone expressing themselves badly.

The Johari Window is a framework for understanding how people see themselves and each other. It sorts information by "Do I know it?" and "Do others know it?" into an open area, a blind spot, a hidden area, and an unknown area, as a way to talk about feedback and appropriate self-disclosure.

The Johari Window uses two questions to divide information into four boxes: Do I know it? Do others know it? What both sides know is the open area. What others see but I don't realize is the blind spot. What I know but haven't told others yet is the hidden area. What neither side knows yet is the unknown area. "Others" here should be understood within a specific relationship and setting.

Listening to specific feedback can turn part of a blind spot into something both sides know. Sharing a bit about your situation can likewise move part of the hidden area into the open. New tasks or experiences can also bring to light abilities and limits no one had noticed before.

A bigger open area isn't automatically better, and it certainly doesn't mean handing over all your privacy. Where it really helps is in letting you check: what do we need to know about each other for this collaboration, and which information gaps could be closed in a suitable way?

In the four-square grid, the columns can show whether you know something or not, and the rows whether others know it or not. Feedback can move things from the blind spot into the open area, and voluntary sharing can move things from the hidden area into the open area. The arrows show information shifting; they aren't a demand to empty every box.
example:
You think you're always good at chiming in with ideas during discussions. One day a coworker gives you feedback: "Twice just now, I hadn't finished talking and you jumped in. After that I didn't really feel like going on." That's different from "You're too pushy," because it describes a specific behavior and its effect, which makes it easier for you to look back on.

You could first check which two moments they mean, then ask them to use an agreed signal to remind you next time. After that, try pausing for two seconds and making sure the other person has finished before you speak, and see whether things improve. Feedback helps you discover a possible blind spot, but you still need to verify the situation rather than treat one observation as a final verdict on who you are.
extra:
On a new project, you're often called on without warning to give a demo. When you're underprepared, you get very nervous, but you've always acted as if it's no big deal, so everyone assumes the arrangement suits you fine. You can choose to share only the part that's relevant to working together: "If I could know the demo topic a day in advance, I'd be able to prepare more thoroughly."

This is sharing your work needs to a suitable degree; you don't have to explain all your personal reasons. Once the information each side has is closer, the arrangements are likely to fit better. You still get to decide what you'd rather keep private and whom you're willing to tell.
steps: Pick a specific relationship and setting, and sort out what relevant information you know and what the other person knows.
Invite the other person to describe specific behaviors and their effects, and share only information you're willing to share that's relevant to working together.
Check the feedback, agree on one small adjustment, then see whether later interactions improve, without rushing to label yourself or anyone else.
caution: It isn't a personality test, and it can't accurately measure how many blind spots someone has. Other people's feedback can also be one-sided or biased, so check it against facts and across different situations. A hidden area isn't the same as lying; keeping things private and declining inappropriate questions are normal boundaries. And the unknown area isn't a blank space for freely guessing at what's going on inside someone else.
exercise: Pick a collaborator you trust and ask: "In our most recent project together, what's one specific thing I did that helped you? What's one thing I could adjust?" Listen all the way through before checking anything, then try one small, fact-based suggestion.
brief: Two stick figures trade puzzle pieces around a half-open shared window. One points out a small patch on the other's back that they can't see, while the other keeps hold of a private box marked with a shield; dashed lines show voluntary sharing and thin arrows show feedback.
diagramCaption: From left to right, the columns show what you know and don't know; from top to bottom, the rows show what others know and don't know. The four boxes are open, blind spot, hidden, and unknown. Solid arrows show feedback; dashed arrows show voluntary sharing.
